title: The Library of Alexandria Didn't Burn Down (Not Like That)
creator: Tomás Reyes
description:
Everyone knows the story of the great fire. The real story of how the Library of Alexandria disappeared is slower, stranger and a lot more relevant.

Further reading:
Roger Bagnall, Alexandria: Library of Dreams
Lionel Casson, Libraries in the Ancient World

sentences.t: Everybody knows the story.
There was this magnificent library in ancient Egypt that held all the knowledge of the ancient world, and then one day it burned, and humanity got set back a thousand years.
It's a great story.
It's also, mostly, not what happened.
And the real version is, I think, way more interesting, and honestly way more relevant to us right now.
So let's start at the beginning.
Alexandria was founded by Alexander the Great in 331 BC, but he never saw it finished, because he died about eight years later.
After his death, his generals carved up his empire, and Egypt went to a man named Ptolemy.
Ptolemy and his son wanted Alexandria to be the intellectual capital of the Greek world, and they were willing to pay for it.
So they built what was called the Mouseion, the shrine of the Muses, which was less a library and more a research institute.
Scholars were invited from all over the Mediterranean, given salaries, free meals, and housing, and basically told to think.
The library was one part of that complex.
How big was it?
Ancient sources throw around numbers like four hundred thousand scrolls, or even seven hundred thousand.
Modern historians are pretty skeptical of those numbers, but even a fraction of that would have made it the largest collection anywhere at the time.
And the way they built that collection is wild.
According to one story, every ship that docked in Alexandria was searched for books.
Any scrolls found on board were taken to the library and copied, and then the library kept the original and handed the owners the copy.
In another story, the Ptolemies borrowed the official copies of the great Athenian plays, put down a huge deposit, and then simply never returned them, happily giving up the money.
Whether or not every detail is true, it tells you how seriously they took this.
And the people who worked there were extraordinary.
Eratosthenes, who ran the library at one point, worked out the circumference of the Earth using shadows and a bit of geometry, and got remarkably close.
Scholars there edited the first standard versions of Homer, which is part of why we can read the Iliad the way we do today.
And translators in the city produced the first Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint, which became hugely important for early Christianity.
So this was a real place, doing real work.
The question is, what happened to it?

Okay, so what happened to the library?
The most famous suspect is Julius Caesar.
In 48 BC, Caesar was trapped in Alexandria during a civil war, and he set fire to ships in the harbor.
The fire spread to the docks, and ancient writers say books were burned, but it's very possible those were scrolls sitting in warehouses near the water, not the library itself.
We know scholars were still working in Alexandria long after Caesar left.
The real damage was slower.
In 145 BC, a century before Caesar, a king named Ptolemy the Eighth purged the city's intellectuals, and the head librarian fled.
After that, the library never really attracted the same talent again.
Then came the Romans, who cared less about funding Greek scholars, and over the following centuries the money dried up.
In the 270s AD, fighting under the emperor Aurelian wrecked the palace quarter where the library likely stood.
And in 391, a daughter library at the temple of Serapis was destroyed during religious conflict in the city.
The famous story about the Arab conquest in the 600s, with a caliph ordering the books burned, was written centuries later and most historians treat it as a legend.
So there was no single fire.
There was a long, quiet decline, where funding was cut, scholars left, and nobody thought it was their job to keep copying the scrolls.
And that's the part that feels relevant, because knowledge rarely disappears in one dramatic moment, it disappears when people stop maintaining it.
Think about how many websites from fifteen years ago are already gone.
If you want to go deeper, I've put two great books in the description.
